(1) When the Brooklyn Bridge opened in 1883, it was the longest suspension bridge in the world, stretching more than a mile from Manhattan to Brooklyn. (2) Most people know that the bridge was designed by John A. Roebling and completed by his son, Washington. (3) Fewer people know that Washington's wife, Emily Warren Roebling, played a major role in finishing it, even though she had no training as an engineer.

(4) Washington Roebling took charge of the project in 1869 after his father died from an injury he suffered while surveying the site. (5) For the next few years, Washington spent long hours in the caissons, the huge airtight chambers where workers dug the bridge's foundations beneath the East River. (6) In 1872, he developed caisson disease, a painful and sometimes deadly illness caused by leaving a high-pressure space too quickly. (7) He was too sick to visit the construction site and could only watch the work through a telescope from his window. (8) Emily began carrying his instructions to the engineers and workers each day, and she brought their reports and questions back to him.

(9) Emily soon realized that she could not explain her husband's ideas unless she understood them herself. (10) She studied higher mathematics. (11) She also studied the strength of materials and the construction of steel cables. (12) Before long, the engineers who worked under her husband was bringing their questions directly to her. (13) The East River is actually a tidal strait, not a true river. (14) Some people even began to suspect that Emily, not Washington, was the real chief engineer of the bridge.

(15) When the bridge was finally ready in 1883, Emily became the first person to ride across it in a carriage, more than ten years after her husband had fallen ill. (16) She carried a rooster with her as a symbol of victory.
Question: Which transition should be added to the beginning of sentence 7?
Explanation: To choose a transition, decide how the two sentences are related. Sentence 6 states a cause: in 1872, Washington developed caisson disease. Sentence 7 states the effect: he was too sick to visit the construction site. A cause-and-effect transition is needed, so "As a result," is correct.
Common Trap: Students who do not reread sentence 6 sometimes choose "Nevertheless" because they expect a transition to signal a turn in the story. The real turn comes in sentence 8, when Emily steps in. Sentence 7 simply follows from the illness, so it needs a cause-and-effect transition, not a contrast.

Author: Jed Levine
Passage:
(1) On a hot summer afternoon, the temperature inside a honeybee hive can climb quickly, especially when thousands of busy bees are crowded together. (2) However, the bees must keep the brood area, where eggs hatch and young bees develop, close to 95 degrees Fahrenheit. (3) If the hive becomes much warmer than that, the developing bees can be harmed or even killed. (4) To prevent this from happening, honeybees work together cooperatively as a team to cool their home.

(5) The first method bees use is fanning. (6) Worker bees line up at the entrance of the hive, face the same direction, and beat their wings rapidly. (7) This movement pushes hot air out of the hive, it also pulls cooler air in from outside.

(8) When fanning alone is not enough to cool the hive, bees turn to a second method. (9) Forager bees fly to nearby ponds, streams, and puddles and carry water back to the hive in their bodies. (10) They spread thin films of the water across the tops of the honeycomb cells. (11) As the fanning bees blow air across these films, the water evaporates and carries heat away with it.

(12) A third method is surprisingly simple: some of the bees leave the hive for a while. (13) On very hot evenings, hundreds of bees may gather in a thick cluster on the outside of the hive, a behavior that beekeepers call "bearding." (14) With fewer bodies crowded inside, the hive produces less heat. (15) Honey found in ancient Egyptian tombs was still safe to eat thousands of years later. (16) Together, these methods make honeybees remarkably skilled at controlling the temperature of their home, even during the hottest weeks of summer.
Question: Which revision of sentence 4 is the most concise without changing its meaning?
Choice A: To prevent this from happening, honeybees cooperate together as a team to cool their home.
Choice C: To prevent this from happening, honeybees, working together cooperatively, cool their home as a team.
Choice D: To prevent this, honeybees work together to cool their home.
Explanation: Sentence 4 says the same thing three times: "work together," "cooperatively," and "as a team." The phrase "from happening" is also unnecessary because "prevent this" already means it. Choice D keeps only one way of saying "work together" and keeps the purpose, "to cool their home," so it is concise without losing meaning.
Common Trap: Choice B is tempting because it is the shortest. But concise does not mean shortest. A concise revision removes repeated or empty words while keeping all of the important information, and choice B loses the reason the bees work together.
Choice A Explanation: "Cooperate together" and "as a team" both repeat the idea of working together, so this choice is still wordy.
Choice B Explanation: This choice is short, but it drops the purpose of the teamwork. The reader no longer knows that the bees are trying to cool the hive.
Choice C Explanation: This choice rearranges the words but keeps every repeated idea: "together," "cooperatively," and "as a team."
Choice D Explanation: Correct. This choice removes the unneeded words "from happening," "cooperatively," and "as a team" while keeping the full meaning.

Choice A: The High Line shows that an old thing nobody uses anymore can become something very, very good for a city.
Choice B: The High Line shows that old stuff in a city can turn into nice things for everyone.
Choice C: The High Line shows that an abandoned piece of a city's past can become a beloved public space.
Choice D: The High Line shows that an old thing that nobody uses anymore can become something extremely positive and great for a city.
Explanation: Sentence 17 uses vague words: "an old thing" and "something really good." A precise revision names exactly what the writer means. The old thing is an abandoned railroad structure from the city's past, and it became a public park that people love. Choice C says this in specific words and connects to the history and popularity described in the passage.
Common Trap: Choice D is tempting because it sounds more forceful than the original. But adding words like "extremely" and "great" only increases emphasis. Precision comes from replacing vague nouns with specific ones, not from piling on adjectives.
Choice A Explanation: Repeating "very" adds emphasis, but "an old thing" and "something good" are still vague.
Choice B Explanation: "Old stuff" and "nice things" are just as vague as the original, and the words are too casual for a report.
Choice C Explanation: Correct. "An abandoned piece of a city's past" precisely describes the unused tracks, and "a beloved public space" precisely describes the park that millions now visit.
Choice D Explanation: "Extremely positive and great" makes the sentence longer but not more specific. It still does not say what the old thing became.
